title: English Sectional (75 Day Practice Mix) — Mock #6

questions.q_en:
Renewable energy is often presented as an uncomplicated remedy to the twin crises of climate change and energy insecurity. Governments announce ambitious targets, corporations highlight sustainability commitments, and public discourse treats renewables as an inevitable successor to fossil fuels. Yet this narrative of inevitability conceals a more complex reality. Transitioning to renewable energy is not merely a technological substitution but a structural transformation involving land use, grid stability, economic redistribution, and political negotiation. Ignoring these dimensions risks replacing one form of dependency with another. One persistent challenge lies in intermittency. Solar and wind energy, while abundant, are not continuously available, requiring storage systems or backup infrastructure. Although technological advances have reduced costs, large-scale storage remains economically and logistically constrained. As a result, renewable integration often relies on conventional energy sources during periods of low generation. This dependence complicates claims of energy independence and exposes the limits of viewing renewables as a standalone solution.

Social and environmental trade-offs further complicate the transition. Large renewable projects demand vast land areas, sometimes displacing communities or disrupting local ecosystems. Ironically, projects designed to mitigate environmental harm can generate localized ecological and social resistance. When decision-making excludes affected populations, renewable energy risks replicating the extractive logic historically associated with fossil fuels—only under a different moral banner.

The long-term success of renewable energy, therefore, depends less on technological optimism and more on institutional capacity. Transparent governance, adaptive grid management, and equitable distribution of costs and benefits are critical. Without these, renewable energy may expand in capacity yet fall short in legitimacy, provoking resistance that slows the very transition it seeks to accelerate.

options_en: Each of the senior researchers who were painstakingly
assigned to the multi-disciplinary international climate project
were asked to submit his findings by the end of the quarter
No Error
options_hi: Each of the senior researchers who were painstakingly
assigned to the multi-disciplinary international climate project
were asked to submit his findings by the end of the quarter

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C).

Replace “were asked” with “was asked”

Rule / Concept: Use of "Each" -

The distributive pronoun "Each" is always considered a singular subject. When a sentence follows the structure "Each of + Plural Noun," the plural noun is simply part of a prepositional phrase. The verb must ignore that plural noun and agree with "Each."

Analysis of the Complexity - This question is a "double-trap" because it contains two different verbs that look like they might be errors, but only one is.

This is CORRECT. The word "who" refers back to "researchers" (plural). Therefore, the verb inside this specific clause must be plural.

This is INCORRECT. This verb belongs to the subject "Each." Because "Each" is singular, the verb must be "was asked."

Corrected Sentence - Each of the senior researchers who were painstakingly assigned to the multi-disciplinary international climate project was asked to submit his findings by the end of the quarter.

questions.q_en: __________ you had finished your homework, you went out to play.
questions.q_hi: __________ you had finished your homework, you went out to play.
options_en: As soon as
No sooner
Both A and C
options_hi: As soon as
No sooner
Both A and C
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option D

Why? Because the sentence is in the simple past and lacks inversion. If it said "Had you finished", then "No sooner" would be the only choice. Since it says "you had finished", both "As soon as" and "Once" are grammatically sound.

👉 Both “As soon as” and “Once” are grammatically correct.

📌 Rule / Concept: Temporal Conjunctions vs. Negative Inversion

This question is a "trap" because it tests your ability to distinguish between a standard Subject + Verb sentence and an Inverted sentence.

Standard Structure (A & C): These conjunctions follow the normal word order: Conjunction + Subject + Verb.

Inversion Structure (B): "No sooner" requires the auxiliary verb to come before the subject (e.g., No sooner had you finished...).

✅ Correct Sentence: As soon as (OR) Once you had finished your homework, you went out to play.

options_en: While many teenagers are obsessed with high-end
smartphones, my younger brother still prefers a laptop to
tablet for his academic research and programming projects.
options_hi: While many teenagers are obsessed with high-end
smartphones, my younger brother still prefers a laptop to
tablet for his academic research and programming projects.
questions.solution_en:
Replace “tablet” with “a tablet”.

Rule / Concept: Parallelism of Articles with Countable Nouns in a Comparison –

When two singular countable nouns are compared or used in a parallel structure (such as with the verb "prefer"), they must both be accompanied by their respective articles. If the first noun takes an indefinite article (a/an), the second noun must also take an indefinite article to maintain grammatical symmetry and clarity, provided they are being used in a general sense.

Corrected Sentence- While many teenagers are obsessed with high-end smartphones, my younger brother still prefers a laptop to a tablet for his academic research and programming projects.

More Examples for Clarity-

1. She prefers a pen to a pencil for writing her diary.

2. I prefer the city life to the country life. (Specific/Definite comparison)

Things to Remember / Exam Tips -

Countable vs. Uncountable: This rule applies to countable nouns. If you say "I prefer tea to coffee," no article is needed because they are uncountable. But for "bike" and "scooty," articles are mandatory.

The Sound Trap: If the second noun starts with a vowel sound, use "an" even if the first one used "a" (e.g., a laptop to an iPad).

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: Due to the integration of advanced neural networks, most
modern supercomputers now process highly complex
algorithms so fastly that users perceive absolutely no lag.
options_hi: Due to the integration of advanced neural networks, most
modern supercomputers now process highly complex
algorithms so fastly that users perceive absolutely no lag.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C) Replace “fastly” with “fast”.

Rule / Concept: Identical Adjective and Adverb Forms

In English grammar, certain words are categorized as "flat adverbs" or words with identical forms. This means they function as both an adjective (modifying a noun) and an adverb (modifying a verb) without any change in spelling. The word "fast" is a primary example. Unlike "slow" which becomes "slowly," "fast" remains "fast" in both roles.

These words have same adjective and adverb forms :-

Fast, hard, late, straight, daily, weekly, monthly, yearly etc

Application to the Given Question

"...process highly complex algorithms so fastly that users perceive absolutely no lag."

In this sentence, the word modifies the verb "process." Since it describes the manner of the action, an adverb is required. However, because "fast" is its own adverbial form, adding "-ly" creates a non-standard word. This is a classic "trap" question designed to see if a candidate blindly applies the "-ly" suffix rule to all adverbs.

Corrected Sentence

Due to the integration of advanced neural networks, most modern supercomputers now process highly complex algorithms so fast that users perceive absolutely no lag.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1: He drove a fast car. (Adjective) ✅

Example 2: He drove the car very fast. (Adverb) ✅

Example 3: We need to make a fast decision. (Adjective) ✅

incorrect Usage

Wrong example 1: The news spread fastly across the internet. ❌

Wrong example 2: A fastly moving object was spotted in the sky. ❌

options_en: guilty about / guilty of

options_hi: guilty about / guilty of

guilty of / guilty of

questions.solution_en:
Rule

Application to the Given Question

"The defendant was found [1] guilty of the heist... he continued to feel [2] guilty about the trauma..."

First Blank: The context is a jury's verdict regarding a "heist" (a crime). This is a statement of legal fact, requiring the preposition "of."

Second Blank: The context is the person's internal "feelings" regarding the "trauma" (remorse). Since it describes a psychological state of regret, we use "about."

questions.q_en: He has a sound understanding of fiscal policy and macroeconomic stability, ______?
questions.q_hi: He has a sound understanding of fiscal policy and macroeconomic stability, ______?
options_en: hasn’t he
doesn’t he
didn’t he
isn’t he
options_hi: hasn’t he
doesn’t he
didn’t he
isn’t he
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) - “doesn’t he”.

📌 Rule / Concept: “Have” as Main Verb (Possession) vs Auxiliary Verb

When “have” is used as a main verb to indicate possession, the question tag is generally formed using do-support (do/does/did) in formal competitive exam English.

However, when “have” is used as an auxiliary verb (e.g., in present perfect tense), we repeat have/has/had in the tag.

💢 Application to the Given Question - Here, “has” expresses possession, not present perfect tense. So, we treat it like a simple present verb.

  • Subject = he

  • Tense = present

  • No auxiliary used (since “has” is main verb here)

  • Therefore → use doesn’t he?

So, the correct tag is: doesn’t he?

✅ More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅ - She has a valid passport, doesn’t she?

Example 2 ✅ - They have sufficient evidence, don’t they?

Example 3 ✅- He has strong analytical skills, doesn’t he?

🧠 Things to Remember

  • “Have” = possession → use do/does/did in tag (preferred in exams).

  • “Have” = auxiliary (has finished) → repeat has/have.

  • Always check whether “have” is main verb or helping verb.

Rule / Concept: Must (Logical Deduction / Strong Probability) –

In English grammar, "Must" is used not only for obligation but also to express a strong logical conclusion or deduction based on available evidence. When we are almost 100% certain that something is true because of the facts, we use "must." When referring to the past, the structure used is Must + have + V3.

Application to the Given Question –

In this sentence, the "jury" is making a logical deduction based on two strong pieces of evidence:

1. The presence of fingerprints on the weapon, and

2. The lack of an alibi. These facts lead to a near-certain conclusion. Options like "should" (advice) or "can" (general ability) do not fit the context of a logical legal conclusion based on evidence.

More Examples for Clarity -

  1. The ground is wet; it must have rained last night. (Deduction based on wet ground) ✔

  2. He hasn't eaten all day; he must be starving. (Deduction based on hunger) ✔

Things to Remember / Exam Tips -

  1. Evidence-Based: If the sentence provides a "reason" or "fact" before the blank (like fingerprints, wet ground, etc.), look for Must to show the logical result.

  2. Must have + V3: This is the standard form for making deductions about the past.

  3. Must vs. May/Might: Use 'Must' for 90-100% certainty; use 'May/Might' for 30-50% uncertainty.

Rule/Concept: Might (Remote Possibility in Conditionals) -

'Might' is used to express a very weak or remote possibility. In the context of Conditional Type 3 (past unreal situations), we use the structure: If + Subject + had + V3, Subject + might + have + V3.

Application to the Given Question - The sentence uses an inverted conditional structure ("Had the investigators arrived" instead of "If the investigators had arrived"). It describes a past possibility that did not happen. 'Might' correctly fits the "remote possibility" required by the context of a near-miss at a crime scene.

More Examples for Clarity-

  1. If I had worked harder, I might have passed the exam. (Possibility)

  2. If it had rained, the match might have been cancelled. (Remote chance)

Things to Remember / Exam Tips-

  1. Remote vs. Strong: Use 'May' for a 50% chance and 'Might' for a 20-30% chance.

  2. Inversion Trap: "Had + Subject + V3" is just a formal way of writing "If + Subject + had + V3". Don't let the lack of "If" confuse you.

  3. Past Tense of May: In Indirect Speech, 'May' always changes to 'Might'. (e.g., He said that it might rain).

Rule/Concept: Linking Verb + Used (Adjective) + To (Preposition) –

In this structure, "used" functions as an adjective meaning "accustomed to" or "familiar with." It is preceded by a linking verb (is/am/are/was/were/get/become) and followed by the preposition "to". Because "to" is a preposition here, it must be followed by a Noun, Pronoun, or Gerund (V1+ing).

Application to the Given Question - In question, the sentence describes a state of being familiar with a difficult activity. The word following the blank is "trekking" (a Gerund/V1+ing). Only the "be used to" structure can grammatically precede a gerund in this context.

More Examples for Clarity -

  1. I am used to the loud noise of the city now. (Used to + Noun)

  2. She is used to working under immense pressure. (Used to + Gerund)

Things to Remember / Exam Tips -

  1. The V1+ing Trigger: If you see a verb ending in -ing immediately after the blank, you almost certainly need a linking verb (is/am/are/was/were) before "used to."

  2. The "To" Nature: Remember that in "I used to go," 'to' is part of the infinitive. In "I am used to going," 'to' is a preposition.

  3. "Get" vs "Be": "Be used to" describes a state (already familiar), while "Get used to" describes the process (becoming familiar).

Rule / Concept: Articles with Ordinal Numbers and Possessive Adjectives –

Ordinal numbers (First, Second, Third, Next, Last, etc.) are normally preceded by the definite article 'the' because they point to a specific position in a sequence. However, a grammatical conflict occurs when a Possessive Adjective (my, our, your, his, her, its, their) is used. Since both a possessive adjective and a definite article are "determiners," they cannot be used together before the same noun. In such cases, the possessive adjective takes precedence, and the article 'the' must be omitted.

Corrected Sentence- It is imperative for the security personnel to understand that their first responsibility during a fire drill is to guide the employees toward the nearest emergency exit.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (D)

📌 Rule / Concept: Verbs of Perception (See, Hear, Watch) – Active to Passive Conversion

With verbs of perception, the active structure may be: Subject + saw + object + base verb (bare infinitive) or Subject + saw + object + V-ing. In passive voice, when the active sentence uses the bare infinitive (enter), the structure becomes: Object + was/were + seen + to + base verb. However, English also allows the -ing form in passive (was seen entering), especially when emphasizing the action in progress. Both structures are grammatically acceptable depending on nuance.

📌 Application to the Given Question

The security personnel saw the intruder enter the server room. Here, “saw” is in the simple past tense and is followed by object + bare infinitive (“enter”). In passive voice, the correct formal transformation is: “The intruder was seen to enter the server room.” Additionally, English permits: “The intruder was seen entering the server room,” which emphasizes the action in progress. Option (A) is incorrect because “to” is missing. Hence, both (B) and (C) are correct.

💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

After verbs of perception, add “to” before the verb in passive if the active uses the bare infinitive. The -ing form is also acceptable in many contexts. Maintain the original tense. Watch carefully for omission of “to,” which makes the sentence incorrect.
